reasons.C1: Collusion detection on real public payment ledgers is a neglected, operator-relevant problem; but wallets are not shown to be LLM agents.
reasons.C2: Held-out families, permutation test and synthetic positive control are solid; labels share the rule's evidence and independent-feature rule drops to p = 0.14.
reasons.C3: Report present with clear numbers, but 17 pages against an 8-page cap dilutes the core result.

levers.C1: Show flagged wallets are actually LLM agents, for example via agent registry or call metadata, tying the detector to AI collusion.
levers.C2: Obtain labels from an independent team whose evidence is disjoint from the rule's features, and test on more held-out families.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages with one headline table: held-out accuracy, independent-feature result, spot-check and synthetic ring recovery.

K5.verdict: Most deployable entry: a real ledger detector with honest controls, but label leakage and unverified agent identity cap its strength.

reasons.C1: Rival coalitions against each other is a fresh framing, though coalitions are instructed rather than emergent.
reasons.C2: 144 real episodes, pre-registration with hashes and a no-rival arm; no positive control, post-freeze measure change, key effect p = 0.055.
reasons.C3: Report not seen and no limitations or dual-use appendix; findings scattered across tables and README.

levers.C1: Let blocs form without instruction and show rivalry changes cohesion, turning a framing into a finding about emergent collusion.
levers.C2: Add a positive control arm with known collusion, more seeds per cell, and report the pre-freeze defection measure alongside the corrected one.
levers.C3: Deliver the report with a limitations and dual-use appendix and one figure summarising outcome classes by cell.

J6.verdict: Interesting question and careful pre-registration, but no positive control and a missing report leave it hard to trust or read.

reasons.C1: Say-versus-do measurement of accepting a secret price-fixing offer is reasonable, close to existing LLM pricing-collusion work.
reasons.C2: Strong test scaffolding and frozen preregistration, but no real model run, no model chosen, no results.
reasons.C3: Design is described, but no report or results exist to communicate findings.

levers.C1: Show a real gap between stated acceptance and pricing behaviour across model families, with a detection implication for monitors.
levers.C2: Run the 60 planned games on real models, pass the positive control, and report Wilson intervals per condition.
levers.C3: Write the report with a results table per condition and a clear statement of what sellers said versus did.

M3.verdict: Well-engineered harness with nothing measured yet; forty hours out, this is still a plan.

reasons.C1: First direct test of fines, leniency and rewards on LLM cartels against a human benchmark; directly useful to authorities.
reasons.C2: Real runs, scripted baselines, positive control, recall check; only one model family, 4 pools and 18 pending result marks.
reasons.C3: Report and eight-panel human-versus-agent figure are clear, but over the cap with many placeholders.

levers.C1: Show which enforcement regime fails on agents and why, with a policy recommendation that differs from the human evidence.
levers.C2: Complete the known-effect arms, add a second provider and more pools to narrow intervals.
levers.C3: Fill every placeholder, cut to 8 pages, and lead with the scorecard of reproduced human results.

M7.verdict: Policy-relevant replication with real data and a clean benchmark; credible once pending arms and a second model land.

reasons.C1: Token snapping as a cheap countermeasure is useful, but it is a carrier study with non-adaptive channels and no collusion game.
reasons.C2: Held-out data, text baseline, swapped and shuffled controls, 10 of 10 reproduced checkpoints; channels trained before sprint, no significance tests.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 shows the core result clearly; 13 pages exceed the cap and the collusion link is underexplained.

levers.C1: Train channels adaptively against snapping and embed them in an actual collusion task to show the countermeasure holds.
levers.C2: Add significance tests, more seeds, and release checkpoints so others can verify without requesting them.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages and state upfront how the vector channel maps onto a concrete agent-collusion threat.

V4.verdict: Rigorous, reproducible countermeasure evidence, but against a non-adaptive channel outside any collusion setting.
